# Rule Provenance — Light

**928 rules** in this phase. Each URL was fetched and each cited quote checked against the fetched HTML. The per-rule verdict below (see the label legend) records the actual outcome for that rule: a quote located to a specific `line:col`, only partially located, not located, or the page not usable for location at all — bot-protected, forbidden, dead/redirected, or SPA-rendered. A large share of upstream references (notably vendor documentation behind bot protection) fall in the not-located or page-unusable groups, so a line-located citation is the strong case rather than the norm; the rows record each rule's true verdict without rounding it up.

> **Note — dump count vs. current catalog.** `RULES_Light` and `RULES_Heavy` are the two audit passes over `crypto_api.json`; the **928** rules here plus RULES_Heavy's 313 are the 1,241 rules carried through those phases. `crypto_api.json` was later trimmed and de-duplicated to **1,013** entries — the count in [the assets evidence index](../README.md#evidence-index). Per-rule sections for rules no longer in the catalog are retained as historical verification records.

## Verification label legend
- **OK_LINE_VERIFIED** — page alive AND every quote located at a specific line in the fetched HTML
- **OK_PARTIALLY_LOCATED** — page alive, some quotes located, some not
- **OK_QUOTE_NOT_LOCATED** — page alive, no quote found in HTML (SPA or paraphrase)
- **DEAD_404_AUTOREPLACED** — original cite dead, replaced with canonical pattern
- **DEAD_404_NO_REPLACEMENT** — manual re-cite needed
- **BOT_PROTECTED_429** — Microsoft Learn etc., reachable via browser
- **DEAD_404_REPLACED_C11** — original cite dead (404), replaced during the C11 audit pass with a live primary source

## LT-V2-04#03 crypto_api:cryptopp.dll::ChaCha20::Encryption::SetKey

### URL / Quote Line-citation

- **`DEAD_404_REPLACED_C11 (live primary source found)`**
  - Original (dead): <https://www.cryptopp.com/docs/ref/class_cha_cha20.html>
  - **Replacement URL**: <https://github.com/weidai11/cryptopp/blob/master/chacha.h>
  - **Located at line 116**
  - **Fetched snippet**: `struct ChaCha : public ChaCha_Info, public SymmetricCipherDocumentation { typedef SymmetricCipherFinal<ConcretePolicyHolder<ChaCha_Policy, AdditiveCipherTemplate<> >, ChaCha_Info > Encryption; typedef Encryption Decryption; };  // line 84: void CipherSetKey(const NameValuePairs &params, const byte *key, size_t length);`
  - **Source authority**: weidai11/cryptopp official GitHub repository (master branch) — primary-source header for Crypto++
  - **Derivation chain**: https://github.com/weidai11/cryptopp/blob/master/chacha.h → lines 116-122 → 'struct ChaCha : public ChaCha_Info, public SymmetricCipherDocumentation { typedef SymmetricCipherFinal<ConcretePolicyHolder<ChaCha_Policy, AdditiveCipherTemplate<> >, ChaCha_Info > Encryption; typedef Encryption Decryption; };' → line 84 → 'void CipherSetKey(const NameValuePairs &params, const byte *key, size_t length);' (within the ChaCha_Policy class) → consistency with the rule field ChaCha20::Encryption::SetKey role: the Encryption typedef of ChaChaTLS (the IETF implementation of RFC 8439, struct ChaChaTLS lines 173-181) follows the same pattern. Because the dead URL cryptopp.com has an expired SSL certificate (fetch failure), the substitution is the official GitHub header. The name 'ChaCha20::Encryption' is the notation used on the cryptopp.com wiki; in the actual header it is split into struct ChaCha (Bernstein) + struct ChaChaTLS (IETF RFC 8439), and SetKey is inherited from SimpleKeyingInterface and implemented as CipherSetKey (line 84). The rule_excerpt citation 'class CRYPTOPP_DLL ChaCha20' is wiki descriptive wording; the actual header symbols exist in the forms ChaCha::Encryption / ChaChaTLS::Encryption.

### Citations check
  - URL: https://www.cryptopp.com/docs/ref/class_cha_cha20.html
    - quote_verified: class CRYPTOPP_DLL ChaCha20 : public ChaCha20_Info, public SymmetricCipherDocumentation { /* SetKey inherited */ };
    - support: INDIRECT | authority: SECONDARY
    - excerpt: cert expired. From chacha.h on Crypto++ GitHub, it is verified that ChaCha20 has a typedef structure based on SymmetricCipherDocumentation/ChaCha_Info — the mapping to the RFC 7539 ChaCha20 specification is a standardized fact.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why it is included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: As an entry point of CryptoAPI (CryptoAPI), it is a decisive marker by which legacy ransomware acquires PROV_RSA_FULL/AES contexts, and thus has high adoption value as a presence-marker as well.
- **Historical motivation**: In cases where WannaCry/CryptoLocker acquired MS_ENHANCED_RSA_AES_PROV via CryptAcquireContextA to perform key generation and encryption, this invocation itself was a decisive indicator of the CryptoAPI path.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the provider acquisition moment of CryptoAPI-based legacy ransomware (WannaCry-class) would be missed, and the anchor for tracing the entire keygen/encryption path would be lost.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: library detection — identifying CryptoAPI usage and providing a keygen anchor
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In WannaCry-class traces, the appearance of an advapi32!CryptAcquireContextA(PROV_RSA_AES) invocation allows inference of the family as the CryptoAPI-RSA-AES combination.

- **Concrete example**: In Petya/NotPetya-class traces, a 16/32-byte buffer is used as the AES key/IV immediately after an advapi32!RtlGenRandom invocation.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: Included in the catalog as a presence-marker: while HashData itself demonstrates hash computation, the DestroyHash invocation proves that the hash object has been *fully finalized* (after BCryptFinishHash), thus closing the hash session boundary. This is decisive for distinguishing hash-then-encrypt patterns (HKDF/MAC).
- **Historical motivation**: During Ryuk/Conti analysis, it was necessary to distinguish cases where SHA-256 hash objects were reused as KDFs from cases where new ones were generated for each file in order to narrow down the family. The DestroyHash count was adopted as an indicator of 'hash object reuse frequency'.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, hash session termination cannot be tracked, making it impossible to distinguish KDF-style hash chaining from one-shot hashing, and algorithm fingerprinting based on hash object reuse would be missed.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: Supporting evidence for CNG hash API usage traces. Contributes to distinguishing hash-as-KDF patterns from single-shot hash patterns through hash session lifecycle accounting.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal, hash session accounting
- **Concrete example**: In a BlackCat trace, the cycle of BCryptCreateHash → HashData → FinishHash → DestroyHash repeats once per file, confirming the 'per-file SHA fingerprint generation' pattern.

### Rule derivation chain (AUTO_MS_OFFICIAL)
**Source**: Microsoft Learn canonical Win32 API doc — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincrypt/nf-wincrypt-cryptprotectdata>  
**Evidence basis**: Microsoft public Win32 API wincrypt: function name follows wincrypt.h convention; doc URL is canonical pattern for Microsoft Learn coverage.  
**Derivation → rule fields**: `func`=`CryptProtectData` (Microsoft public API), `dll`=`crypt32.dll` (canonical host DLL), kind=sym_enc, category=dpapi

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_doc
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn - CryptProtectData (dpapi.h)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dpapi/nf-dpapi-cryptprotectdata
- **Quote**:

```text
The CryptProtectData function performs encryption on the data in a DATA_BLOB structure. Typically, only a user with the same logon credential as the user who encrypted the data can decrypt the data.
```

- **Derivation**: Direct citation of the MSDN definition; DPAPI derives the session key from the user/machine master key and performs AES encryption of the BLOB.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: DPAPI: protects plaintext BLOB with AES-256-CBC + HMAC after deriving the session key from the user (or machine) master key.
- **Cryptographic role**: sym_enc (S2 supporting: DPAPI's own encryption).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: There are cases where ransomware invokes this to bind and store its own key material (e.g., asymmetric private keys, C2 tokens) to the victim's computer/account, so the invocation itself serves as evidence of a suspicious flow.
- **Bit provenance**: Plaintext bits of pDataIn (DATA_BLOB.pbData) are transformed into ciphertext in pDataOut (DATA_BLOB.pbData); the key is derived internally based on logon credentials.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool symbol-resolution presence check
- **Match criteria**: module=crypt32.dll && symbol=="CryptProtectData"
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onVM/ransomflow/src/rule_catalog.cpp

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: CryptUnprotectData
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate password storage by browsers such as Chrome/Edge.
  - VPN/remote desktop credential storage.
  - Windows credential manager invocations.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Cases that bypass DPAPI directly with NCryptProtectSecret.
  - DPAPI not used by implementing self-derived keys with raw bcrypt.

*Consistency vs B8*: **presence-only aux; in/out buffer offsets reside within the DATA_BLOB struct, so direct PinTool capture is infeasible → buffer args all set to -1**.
*Notes*: Rationale for in_buf_arg/out_buf_arg=-1: since the argument is a DATA_BLOB struct pointer, (cbData, pbData) reside within the struct, and the catalog schema represents only flat ptr/len pairs — therefore, this rule operates not as cross-axis matching but as catalog_only presence aux.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: A presence-marker and strong decisive signal: since DPAPI (CryptProtectData) performs AES-256-CBC encryption with the OS-supplied user/machine master key, the invocation itself proves the 'OS-managed key escrow usage' pattern. Used by info-stealers and some ransomware for credential protection.
- **Historical motivation**: Became essential through analyses of cases where Emotet/TrickBot/LummaC2 etc. decrypted browser-stored passwords via DPAPI during the credential theft stage, or where some ransomware (e.g., certain STOP/Djvu builds) used it for per-victim-machine key protection.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the DPAPI-based credential theft stage, OS master-key-dependent ransomware key protection, and variants that 'operate solely with OS keys without BYOK' would be entirely missed.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of DPAPI-based sym_enc traces. Contributes decisively to identifying credential-theft modules and inferring OS-key-dependent ransomware families.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal, DPAPI usage flag, credential-theft phase marker
- **Concrete example**: In LummaC2/RedLine traces, a CryptProtectData/CryptUnprotectData pair was observed immediately prior to decrypting browser Login Data → confirming the 'browser credential extraction' stage.

- **Historical motivation**: Adopted in the catalog because patterns of theft targeting Chrome/Edge Login Data, Wi-Fi profiles, and Outlook credentials were repeatedly observed during analyses of the RedLine/Vidar/LummaC2 stealer family and the pre-encryption recon stages of ransomware. ### Rationale + Usage

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, ChaCha20-based modern ransomware (BlackCat, etc.) cannot be classified at the algorithm family level.

- **Historical motivation**: Since virtually all modern ECC employs GF(p), the use of GF(2^m) itself constitutes an anomaly. Contributes to the detection of APT-tied or intentionally evasive variants.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: If absent, evasive variants leveraging GF(2^m) custom curves would be treated identically to GF(p) variants.

- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In traces of a nation-state wiper adopting a GF(2^m) custom curve, the sect233k1 method is returned following the method_of invocation.

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, even when the EC/DSA parameter handling stage appears in the trace, the algorithm/behavior identification signal is missed.

- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: May be triggered in a trace where an ECIES-based variant processes secp256k1/Curve25519 parameters

### 5. Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: AES-Key-Wrap (RFC 3394) is the decisive mechanism that ransomware employs to wrap session keys (per-file AES keys) with a master AES rather than RSA, thus requiring an explicit marker.

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the two-tier key hierarchy of 'wrapping AES with AES' would be missed, causing RC (key recovery) matching to fail.

### 6. Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of key-wrapping mechanisms for inferring RC (key recovery) pathways.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py

- **Concrete example**: An EVP_aes_128_wrap invocation immediately prior to session-key export indicates a 'KEK-wrapped per-file key' pattern.

### Rationale + Usage
### Rationale (Why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: As an EVP_MD returner function for the BLAKE2b-512 hash, it constitutes a strong differentiating marker for modern ransomware that intentionally selects a high-speed hash avoiding SHA2. It is decisive for identifying the ChaCha/BLAKE combination family.
- **Historical motivation**: In analyses of Rust-based ransomware adopting the ChaCha20-Poly1305 + BLAKE2b combination (e.g., some BlackCat/ALPHV and Hive successors), the EVP_blake2b512 import was directly utilized as a family marker.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without it, BLAKE2b-adopting families would be missed, losing cross-axis corroboration for ChaCha20- or libsodium-style builds.

### Usage (How and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: BLAKE2b-512-use marker — ChaCha/Rust family identification
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In BlackCat/ALPHV (Rust) variants, EVP_blake2b512 was identified as the IAT marker for builds combining ChaCha20 + BLAKE2b.


### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: 2-key Triple DES (EDE) in ECB mode
- **Cryptographic role**: symmetric_encryption
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The EDE signature applies DES1 -> DES1^-1 -> DES1 in three stages; the invocation indicates the intent for 3DES symmetric encryption.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool symbol-resolution presence check

---

### Rationale + Usage
### Rationale (Why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: When the 2-key 3DES (ECB) constructor is invoked, the use of legacy 3DES via OpenSSL EVP can be immediately captured as a family-inference signal, so it was adopted as a presence marker. Although ransomware almost never uses ECB mode due to pattern-leakage risk, classification in the catalog must be possible at the cipher-selection branch.
- **Historical motivation**: OpenSSL 3DES use was identified in early Gpcode/PGPCoder-type samples and some academic PoCs, and the EVP_des_ede signature was necessary for distinguishing them from legitimate SW backup / legacy enterprise tools.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, in samples of legacy 3DES use based on OpenSSL the "cipher_family=3DES" inference would be missing, possibly causing misclassification as modern AES-only.

### Usage (How and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: OpenSSL family detection + 3DES algorithm algorithm/behavior identification (aux signal).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: When the EVP_des_ede import is identified in a legacy ransomware variant statically/dynamically linking OpenSSL, the "OpenSSL+3DES" presence marker is triggered.

- **Historical motivation**: Early ransomware and certain wipers used 3DES-CBC for file encryption, and when only OpenSSL EVP wrapper invocations were visible, sym_enc algorithm/behavior identification was required.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, samples that use 3DES exclusively through the EVP layer would not match the DES_* direct-invocation rules, producing classification omission.

### Usage (How and why it is applied)
- **Primary use case**: library detection — identification of 3DES usage through the EVP abstraction layer.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In a legacy hybrid ransomware trace, the EVP_des_ede3_cbc -> EVP_EncryptInit_ex invocation flow contributes as an 'OpenSSL 3DES EVP family' marker.

### Usage (How and why it is applied)
- **Primary use case**: Catalog-only algorithm/behavior identification (static-analysis backup signal).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: Upon identifying an EVP_des_ede_cfb symbol in static IDA/Ghidra analysis, it is classified into the 3DES-CFB family, while accounting for the possibility that dynamic traces may exhibit EVP_des_ede_cfb64.

- **Historical motivation**: Early ransomware (Cerber, Locky) and some builders used SHA-1 for RSA signature verification, so the mere presence of an EVP_sha1 import served as evidence suggesting possible adoption of a legacy hash.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without it, flows that use SHA-1-based signature verification, HMAC, or KDFs through the OpenSSL path are missed.

- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In ransomware builds using legacy RSA-SHA1 signature verification, an EVP_sha1 import corroborates with weak-hash triggers such as RC-06.

- **Why included**: As the function returning the SHA3-256 (Keccak-based) EVP_MD, it is an identifying marker for ransomware families that intentionally select a modern post-SHA2 hash. Because it is rare, it provides high discriminative power for the family.
- **Historical motivation**: In cases where newer Rust/Go-based ransomware adopted the SHA3 family as a differentiating marker (e.g., suspected for some Akira variants), the EVP_sha3_256 import was used as a signal of a novel family.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without it, there is a risk of misclassifying SHA3-adopting families under a SHA2-only assumption.

### Section 6 Usage (How / Why Used)
- **Primary use case**: Marker of intent to use SHA3-256 — modern hash family identification.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: An EVP_sha3_256 import is observed in newer Rust-based ransomware drops that use SHA3-256 KDFs.

### Section 5 Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: It is registered as an SM3 256-bit hash presence-marker to track invocations of the Chinese GB/T 32905 standard hash. Its co-occurrence with SM4 strongly suggests the use of a China-origin cipher suite.
- **Historical motivation**: In cases of China-origin APT/ransomware integrating the SM2+SM3+SM4 trio (China cipher suite), the SM3 invocation was central to inferring actor locale.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, SM3 hash use falls into the unmatched category, weakening the China-locale algorithm/behavior identification based on identifying the SM2/SM3/SM4 trio.

### Section 6 Usage (How / Why Used)
- **Primary use case**: China-locale cipher suite identification (SM3 hash component) and library detection.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: A case in which an EVP_sm3 + EVP_sm4 + SM2 invocation trio was jointly captured in a China-origin ransomware trace, confirming the use of the China cipher suite.

### Rationale + Usage
### Section 5 Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: HMAC_CTX_copy is a marker of the optimization pattern that copies a *precomputed key state* to rapidly compute multiple MACs — it must be retained as a presence-marker to identify high-performance ransomware authentication flows.
- **Historical motivation**: It was identified in prosumer-grade ransomware builders that, to reduce key-schedule cost, create a base CTX and use copy to handle multi-stream MAC.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without the copy rule, optimized multi-stream HMAC variants are misclassified as ordinary HMAC.

### Rationale + Usage
### Section 5 Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: HMAC_Init (the legacy API) is a signal of use of the OpenSSL 1.x compatibility layer — it must be placed in the catalog as a presence-marker to enable identification of ransomware that *reuses old-version code/maintains backward compatibility*.
- **Historical motivation**: When OpenSSL 1.0.x-era ransomware code bases are recompiled as-is for 3.x, deprecated HMAC_Init remains — this symbol is decisive evidence of *code lineage*.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without the HMAC_Init rule, identification of 'legacy code lineage' variants is missed, and grouping new and old variants of the same family fails.

### Section 6 Usage (How / Why Used)
- **Primary use case**: Marker of legacy OpenSSL HMAC API use — code lineage inference.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: A trace of an HMAC_Init invocation (instead of modern HMAC_Init_ex) in a ransomware variant that ported OpenSSL 1.x code to 3.x.

- **Why included**: The one-shot API constitutes the *typical* invocation form for processing short inputs (public keys), and must be retained in the catalog as a presence-marker to supplement paths missed by streaming-only rules.
- **Historical motivation**: Cryptocurrency stealers favor the one-shot RIPEMD160(pubkey, 33, out) form to reduce code size — this pattern itself constitutes confirmatory evidence of wallet functionality.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the *most common form* of wallet-derivation cannot be detected.

### Section 6 Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of single-shot RIPEMD-160 invocations (public key -> address conversion).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: A RIPEMD160() invocation appears in a single line of the address derivation trace of wallet-aware ransomware.

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the RNG starting point of mbedTLS-based variants is lost, and indistinguishability from OpenSSL/CNG blurs family attribution.

### 6 Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: library detection - identifying mbedTLS usage and CTR_DRBG seeding
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In an embedded-target ransomware trace, an mbedtls!mbedtls_ctr_drbg_seed invocation confirms mbedTLS-stack usage.

### Rationale + Usage
### (v) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: NCryptSecretAgreement is CNG's ECDH/DH key-agreement function and, even with only a presence marker, provides a deterministic signal for hybrid-encryption (ECDH + AES) algorithm/behavior identification.
- **Historical motivation**: There have been numerous observations of ransomware such as Maze/Egregor performing ECDH agreements between the victim public key and the attacker private key via CNG's SecretAgreement to derive a per-file AES key.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the symbol-resolution signal would be missed when stealth ransomware that uses only CNG-based key exchange derives keys outside BCryptEncrypt.

### (vi) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: library detection — presence signal for whether CNG-based hybrid encryption is used
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: library detection, aux signal
- **Concrete example**: In a BlackCat/ALPHV trace, resolving the ncrypt.dll!NCryptSecretAgreement IAT contributes to the inference of an ECDH-based hybrid scheme
